content: Vaginal bleeding or breast enlargement may occur as side effects of treatment. These changes are expected to resolve within the first month of therapy. If they persist beyond two months, it may indicate non-compliance with the treatment regimen or the presence of gonadotropin-independent sexual precocity. If these possibilities are ruled out, the dosage may be increased to 1800 mcg/day, administered as 600 mcg three times daily. Patients experiencing intercurrent rhinitis should consult their physician before using topical nasal decongestants. If a decongestant is necessary during treatment, it should not be used until at least two hours after administering the therapy. Sneezing during or immediately after administration should be avoided, as it may impair drug absorption. Seizures have been reported in patients receiving GnRH agonists, including those with a history of seizures, epilepsy, cerebrovascular disorders, central nervous system anomalies or tumors, and those on concomitant medications associated with seizures (e.g., bupropion, SSRIs). Seizures have also been reported in patients without any of these predisposing conditions. Psychiatric events, including emotional lability (e.g., crying, irritability, impatience, anger, aggression), have been reported in patients taking GnRH agonists. Patients should be monitored for the development or worsening of psychiatric symptoms during treatment. Depression may occur or worsen during therapy, particularly in individuals with a history of depression. Women with new or worsening depression should be referred to a mental health professional as appropriate. Patients should be informed about the potential for depression and advised to report concerning thoughts or behaviors to their healthcare provider immediately. Pseudotumor cerebri (idiopathic intracranial hypertension) has been reported in pediatric patients receiving GnRH agonists, including nafarelin acetate. Patients should be monitored for symptoms such as headache, papilledema, blurred vision, double vision, vision loss, pain behind the eyes or with eye movement, tinnitus, dizziness, and nausea. Patients and caregivers should be informed about the possibility of pseudotumor cerebri. Nafarelin is contraindicated during pregnancy (Pregnancy Category X) due to the potential for harm to the fetus. Its excretion in breast milk is unknown, and breastfeeding is not recommended while using this medication. Nafarelin is a synthetic decapeptide that acts as a GnRH agonist. It desensitizes the pituitary response to endogenous GnRH, leading to reduced secretion of luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), and subsequently decreases ovarian and testicular hormone production. Peak serum levels are achieved within 10–45 minutes, with a half-life of approximately 3 hours. The drug is metabolized by peptidase enzymes and excreted via urine (44–55%) and feces (19–44%). Nafarelin is used in women to treat endometriosis, a condition where uterine lining tissue grows outside the uterus. It is also used in children to treat central precocious puberty (gonadotropin-dependent). The medication mimics the natural hormone GnRH produced by the body. Patients should follow the instructions provided in the Medication Guide and Patient Information Leaflet. Before using the nasal spray for the first time, test sprays should be performed as directed. The nose should be gently blown before administration. The medication is typically used twice daily, approximately 12 hours apart. If multiple sprays are required, a 30-second interval should be observed between sprays. Avoid spraying the medication into the eyes and sneezing during or immediately after use, as this may reduce absorption. Proper cleaning of the spray tip is essential. It is crucial to adhere to the prescribed dosing schedule and not skip doses. Patients should consult their doctor or pharmacist to determine how long each bottle of nasal spray will last. Do not use the bottle beyond the recommended duration, even if medication remains, as the full dose may not be delivered. Do not increase the dose or use the medication more frequently or for longer than prescribed. When starting nafarelin, symptoms may initially worsen (e.g., increased vaginal bleeding in women with endometriosis or signs of puberty in children). These symptoms should improve after the first month of treatment. Common side effects in children include nasal irritation, hot flashes, and vaginal discharge. In women, side effects may include nasal irritation, hot flashes, headaches, decreased sexual interest, muscle pain, vaginal dryness, acne, and reduced breast size. Children may also be at risk for increased intracranial pressure. Serious allergic reactions are rare. Patients should inform their doctor of any allergies, particularly to GnRH or similar hormones (e.g., leuprolide), and disclose all medications and supplements they are taking to avoid potential interactions. Nafarelin may interfere with certain lab tests, such as those assessing pituitary and gonadal function, potentially causing false results. In case of overdose, seek immediate medical attention. In the U.S., contact poison control at 1-800-222-1222. Regular medical and laboratory tests (e.g., growth and bone age velocity in children) should be conducted during treatment. Missed doses should be taken as soon as remembered unless it is near the time for the next dose, in which case the missed dose should be skipped. Store the medication upright at room temperature, away from light and moisture. Do not freeze or store it in the bathroom. Properly discard expired or unused medication as instructed. Always consult your healthcare provider for complete information tailored to your specific health needs.
